props.title: Vernon, Florida
props.initialSlug: Portrait of eccentric Southern life in small-town FL

sections.content: **Vernon, Florida** (1981) stands as one of Errol Morris's earliest and most peculiar documentary achievements. After abandoning his original concept about insurance fraud in the town (where residents allegedly dismembered themselves for insurance money), Morris instead captured the eccentric personalities of this small Southern community. The film's power comes from its deceptively simple approach - letting peculiar characters speak directly to camera about their obsessions, from turkey hunting to growing exotic plants. This established Morris's signature interview style that he'd later perfect in The Thin Blue Line (1988) and **Fast, Cheap & Out of Control** (1997).

sections.content: What makes Vernon, Florida revolutionary is how it avoids the exploitative tendencies common in documentaries about rural America. Unlike later works that mock their subjects like **American Honey** (2016) or **Gummo** (1997), Morris finds dignity and fascination in his subjects' peculiarities. The film pioneered what became known as Morris's "direct cinema" style - prolonged takes of subjects speaking directly to camera, creating an intimacy that reveals profound truths about human nature and obsession.

The film's influence can be seen in later character-driven documentaries like Grey Gardens (1975) and **Sherman's March** (1986), which similarly find extraordinary stories in ordinary places. Morris's technique of letting eccentric personalities simply talk, without narrator intervention, inspired a generation of documentarians including Les Blank and Ross McElwee. sections.content: Morris's approach in Vernon, Florida fundamentally changed how documentarians interact with their subjects. Later works like **The Act of Killing** (2012) and **Stories We Tell** (2012) built on his innovative interviewing techniques. The film's influence extends beyond documentary - you can see its DNA in mockumentaries like **Waiting for Guffman** (1996) and character-driven narratives about small-town America like **Paris, Texas** (1984).
